docs.title: Who the Map Misses
docs.text:
Machine-learning poverty maps are increasingly used to decide where aid goes. This project tests whether they understate deprivation in Indigenous communities, and what that error would cost in a real budget formula.

Mexico is the test bed because its 2020 census reports, for every locality, how many people live in Indigenous households and what infrastructure their dwellings have. That turns the census into ground truth everywhere, so a map's errors can be measured across the whole country instead of at a few survey clusters.

docs.title: What this project does
docs.text:
1. Audits a deployed model. Meta's Relative Wealth Index (RWI) is scored against census ground truth on the same 2.4 km tiles. Errors are compared within the same true wealth decile, which separates an Indigenous-specific blind spot from the known tendency of these maps to pull the poorest places toward the middle, and within the same map decile, which is what someone using the map experiences.
  2. Builds challengers. Models trained on a realistic simulated survey use Google DeepMind's AlphaEarth satellite embeddings (or night lights) and are benchmarked against small area estimation, the statistical method these maps aim to replace.
  3. Tests the label. Asset-based wealth, infrastructure deprivation and a marginalization index are built from the same census to show how the definition of poverty changes who counts as poorest.
  4. Prices the error. Each map is plugged into a stylized version of Mexico's FAIS social-infrastructure formula and a "poorest 20%" targeting rule.
  5. Checks uncertainty for each group. Conformal prediction intervals are evaluated for Indigenous and non-Indigenous localities separately, with and without group-conditional calibration.
  6. Scores each result by the decision it informs. Error measures were fixed in advance: RMSE and signed bias rather than MAPE, compression diagnostics, and paired model comparisons (why).

The hypotheses were written down before the analysis, and the pipeline is validated on synthetic data with biases of known size.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Results: the findings, with every figure next to its table.
  • Methods: definitions, models and design decisions.
  • Lab notebook: how the project developed, one milestone at a time.
  • Reproduce: run everything from raw data.
  • Notebooks: the analysis step by step, from a two-minute synthetic demo to the real-data results.

Scope

Map comparisons cover rural localities (fewer than 2,500 people), which INEGI records as points and which contain most Indigenous-majority communities. Cities need block-level census data; see Methods → Extensions.

docs.title: Processing
docs.text:
1. ITER: drop aggregate rows (municipal totals 0000, pooled one- and two-dwelling localities 9998/9999, state and national totals), convert * and N/D to missing, parse degrees-minutes-seconds coordinates, build the 9-digit cvegeo key.
  2. Shares use occupied private dwellings with recorded characteristics (VIVPARH_CV) as denominator.
  3. Labels: see Methods.
  4. RWI: quadkeys read as text; if leading zeros were stripped (spreadsheets do this, and every Mexican quadkey starts with 0), the zoom is recovered by checking quadkeys against tile coordinates.
  5. Localities are joined to RWI tiles by computing their own quadkey at the RWI zoom.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text:
• Suppression: localities with fewer than three dwellings show only total population and dwellings; they cannot have labels and are excluded from label-based analyses.
  • Point coordinates: one point per locality; see the rural scope in Methods.
  • Vintage mismatch: the RWI was built from 2010s surveys and imagery; the census is from 2020.
  • Coverage: the RWI only covers populated tiles as Meta's population layers saw them. Unmatched localities are a finding (H1), not just missing data.
  • Indigenous identification: household-based and language-based census measures differ, and both differ from self-identification. The pipeline reports both measures.

docs.title: If the RWI does not cover Mexico
docs.text:
Meta's public release describes 93 to 135 low- and middle-income countries depending on the source. If the Mexico file is missing:

  1. Audit NASA SEDAC's Global Gridded Relative Deprivation Index (GRDI), which is global, with the same code: aggregate GRDI to the same tiles and replace rwi with -grdi.
  2. Treat the AlphaEarth-based challenger as the audited system.

Record which path was taken in the deviations log of the pre-analysis plan.

docs.title: What is committed
docs.text: Only aggregated outputs: tables in results/real/tables and figures. No raw files and no locality-level rows are committed.

docs.title: Studying the algorithm, not the communities
docs.text: This project audits a tool and the institutions that use it. It does not build a new instrument for profiling Indigenous communities, and it does not publish rankings of specific localities as candidates for or against programs.

docs.title: Principles followed
docs.text:
The project follows the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance (Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility, Ethics) alongside FAIR data practice:

  • Collective benefit: the question is whether public tools under-serve Indigenous communities, and the main output is evidence that can correct that.
  • Authority to control: only public, aggregated government statistics are used. The census categories are the state's, not the communities' own; that limitation is stated wherever results appear.
  • Responsibility: findings are framed around map and institutional error, not community deficits. Synthetic results are always labeled as synthetic.
  • Ethics: no individual or household data, no re-identification risk, no locality-level outputs committed.

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
• "Indigenous" is capitalized; specific peoples are named where the data allow.
  • Results describe places classified by census measures, not people's identities.
  • Deprivation is described as lack of services the state should provide, not as a trait of a community.

docs.title: Known limits of the categories
docs.text: Household- and language-based census measures undercount people who self-identify as Indigenous, and they treat diverse peoples as one group. Results by people or region would need data the public census tables do not provide.

docs.title: Feedback
docs.text: If you are part of, or work with, an affected community and see a problem with how this work represents it, please open an issue or contact the author. Corrections will be logged.

docs.title: Author's positionality
docs.text: Write a short paragraph about your relationship to this topic and to Indigenous communities, and what you did to check your assumptions. Delete this note.

docs.title: Units and scope
docs.text:
The census reports one row per locality (about 190,000). Meta's Relative Wealth Index (RWI) reports one value per Bing tile at zoom 14 (about 2.4 km). Every locality is assigned to the tile containing its census coordinate, and census quantities are aggregated to tiles with population weights.

ITER gives a single point per locality. That is accurate for rural localities but not for a city spread over dozens of tiles, so map comparisons are restricted to rural localities (fewer than 2,500 people) and to tiles that contain no urban locality.

docs.title: Ground-truth labels
docs.text:
All three labels come from the same census table, so differences between them are differences in definition, not in data.

Label Construction Why it matters Asset wealth (DHS-style) First principal component of shares of dwellings with a fridge, washer, car, computer, cell phone, internet, TV, microwave, electricity, piped water, drainage and a finished floor What the RWI was trained to predict Infrastructure deprivation Mean share of dwellings lacking electricity, piped water, drainage, or with a dirt floor A rate with a direct policy reading; target of FAIS-type spending Marginalization (CONAPO-style) First principal component of illiteracy, incomplete basic education, the four housing deprivations, crowding, and lacking a fridge Mirrors the official index's ingredients

Percentile ranks are population-weighted, so "the poorest 20%" means 20% of people, not of places.

docs.title: Audit of the RWI
docs.text:
Rank error. For tile \(t\), \( e_t = 100\,(\text{RWI percentile}_t - \text{census percentile}_t) \). A positive error means the map ranks the tile as wealthier than the census does.

Within-decile comparison. Machine-learning maps compress the extremes: the poorest places look less poor. Comparing Indigenous and non-Indigenous tiles within the same true decile removes that mechanism from the comparison. Confidence bands come from a municipality-cluster bootstrap.

Regressions. Weighted least squares of \(e_t\) on Indigenous share with cumulative controls (size, remoteness, altitude, true decile, state), weights equal to tile population, standard errors clustered by municipality. Constant controls are dropped automatically.

Coverage. A linear probability model of whether a locality falls inside any RWI tile, on Indigenous share, log population and log distance to the nearest city.

docs.title: Two views of fairness
docs.text:
The same rank errors can be grouped in two ways, and they answer different questions.

View Groups tiles by Question Holds when Separation true (census) decile Among equally poor places, does the map rank Indigenous ones as wealthier? Errors are independent of group, given the truth Calibration map decile Among places the map ranks the same, are Indigenous ones poorer? The truth is independent of group, given the map

When groups differ in average wealth, an imperfect map generally cannot satisfy both (Kleinberg, Mullainathan & Raghavan 2017; Chouldechova 2017). A map whose errors ignore group passes the separation view and still fails the calibration view. If true wealth in group \(g\) is normal with mean \(\mu_g\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), and the map adds noise of variance \(\tau^2\) regardless of group, then among places the map scores \(m\)

\[ E[\text{truth} \mid \text{map} = m,\ g] = \mu_g + k\,(m - \mu_g), \qquad k = \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + \tau^2} < 1, \]

so the group with the lower average is poorer at every map value. The audit therefore uses the separation view for the confirmatory test (H2), because it isolates how the map treats a place given its true condition, and reports the calibration view as what someone who sees only the map experiences. The calibration gap is read against its value in a synthetic world with no planted bias (validation), not against zero.

docs.title: Challenger models
docs.text:
The census is used as a pseudo-census: a realistic household survey is drawn from it (municipalities with probability proportional to population, then localities, then dwellings without replacement), models are trained on the survey only, and predictions are scored against the full census in localities the survey never visited. This mirrors Corral, Henderson & Segovia (2025).

Model Features Borrows strength across localities? Night lights (GBM) VIIRS 2020 average radiance No Embeddings (GBM) 64-d AlphaEarth embedding No Embeddings (GBM + EB) same Yes: empirical-Bayes municipality effects from cross-fitted residuals Embeddings (Fay-Herriot) 20 principal components of the embedding Yes: REML-estimated municipality and locality random effects

Fay-Herriot with a municipality effect. For sampled locality \(i\) in municipality \(j\):

\[ y_{ij} = x_{ij}'\beta + u_j + v_{ij} + e_{ij},\quad u_j\sim N(0,\sigma_u^2),\; v_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma_v^2),\; e_{ij}\sim N(0,\psi_{ij}) \]

with \(\psi_{ij}\) the known design variance of the survey estimate. Each municipality's covariance block \(\sigma_u^2\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}' + \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_v^2+\psi)\) is inverted in closed form (Sherman-Morrison), so REML needs only group sums. Unsampled localities in sampled municipalities receive \(x'\hat\beta + \hat u_j\); others receive \(x'\hat\beta\). The implementation is tested for parameter recovery on simulated data (tests/test_models.py).

docs.title: Evaluation metrics
docs.text:
Each metric was chosen for the decision its output feeds, before any real data were seen (pre-analysis plan §6). The code is in metrics.py.

Accuracy: RMSE first. The budget formula multiplies predicted deprivation rates by population and adds them up, so a prediction has to get the mean right. Squared error is the loss whose best prediction is the mean (it is consistent for the mean; Gneiting 2011), so RMSE is the primary accuracy measure. MAE, whose best prediction is the median, is secondary.

Fairness: signed bias. RMSE and MAE say how far off a model is, not in which direction. Signed bias (prediction minus truth) by group says whether a model systematically understates deprivation for Indigenous localities. It is the H4 metric.

Why not MAPE or MSLE.

Measure Problem on locality deprivation rates MAPE Undefined where the rate is zero, which is common (every dwelling has electricity, say). It divides by the truth, so it weights the least deprived places most. An under-prediction can cost at most 100% while an over-prediction is unbounded (Hyndman & Koehler 2006), so it favors models that understate deprivation: the error under audit. MSLE Built for targets that span orders of magnitude, where relative error matters. A rate between 0 and 1 doesn't, and on that range an error at 100% deprivation counts about a quarter as much as the same error at 0%.

Percentage errors are used only for municipal allocations, which are never close to zero.

People and places. Population-weighted metrics say how wrong a map is for the average person; unweighted ones, for the average community. Indigenous localities are many and small, so a per-person metric can hide large errors in many small places. Both are reported, per person first.

Compression. A model can lower its RMSE by pulling every prediction toward the average, which moves its errors to the extremes, where programs act. Three diagnostics expose this:

  • Calibration slope: the slope of the truth regressed on the prediction. 1 is calibrated; above 1 means the predictions are squeezed toward the average.
  • Variance ratio: the variance of the predictions over the variance of the truth. Below 1 means squeezed.
  • Bias by true decile: compression shows up as positive bias in the least deprived deciles and negative bias in the most deprived.

Intervals. Coverage alone rewards intervals that are too wide; width alone rewards intervals that miss. The interval score (Gneiting & Raftery 2007) combines the two:

\[ S_\alpha(l, u; y) = (u - l) + \frac{2}{\alpha}(l - y)\,\mathbf{1}\{y < l\} + \frac{2}{\alpha}(y - u)\,\mathbf{1}\{y > u\}. \]

Lower is better. It is a proper scoring rule, so a model cannot improve its score by reporting intervals other than its honest ones.

Money. The misallocation share, \(\tfrac12 \sum_j |\hat s_j - s_j|\) over municipal budget shares, is the fraction of the budget that would have to move to reproduce the census-based allocation. It is reported with the net change for Indigenous-majority municipalities and the median absolute percentage error by municipality.

Comparing models. In each replication every model is trained and scored on the same simulated survey, so differences are taken replication by replication and the luck of the draw cancels. Tables report the mean paired difference, its 2.5th-97.5th percentiles across replications, and the share of replications in which a model does worse.

Tests. H1 (two-sided) and H2 (one-sided, as pre-registered) are adjusted together with Holm's method. Everything else is an estimate with an uncertainty range.

Denominators. A metric exists only where the truth is known. Each analysis reports the share of the in-scope population it covers, by group. Localities with suppressed census data (fewer than three dwellings) also lack Indigenous status, so they appear as a separate "Unknown" group instead of disappearing from the denominator.

docs.title: Prediction intervals
docs.text: Split conformal intervals use cross-fitted residuals on surveyed localities as calibration scores. Three versions: marginal (one quantile), Mondrian by group, and Mondrian by group × size tercile. Coverage, width and interval score are reported separately for localities inside the survey frame (at least 10 dwellings) and outside it, because conformal guarantees require calibration and test points to be exchangeable.

docs.title: Allocation
docs.text:
• Targeting: select the localities predicted to be most deprived until 20% of the rural population is covered; the exclusion rate is the share of the truly poorest population left out.
  • Formula: split a fixed budget across municipalities in proportion to the estimated number of deprived people (population × deprivation rate). This follows the logic of Mexico's FAIS, which allocates by extreme poverty weighted by average deprivations; it is a stylized rule, not the legal formula.
  • The RWI is relative, so it is converted to a deprivation rate by quantile-mapping its ranks onto the national distribution of the census rate (as if that distribution were known from a survey).
  • Errors: the misallocation share and municipal percentage errors (see Evaluation metrics).

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: mapaudit validate generates synthetic worlds with and without a planted Indigenous bias and checks that the audit finds it only when it is there. The same check runs in CI (tests/test_validation.py). The world without bias also supplies the benchmark for the calibration view, and a test checks that this view shows a gap the separation view does not (tests/test_metrics.py).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Census labels describe dwellings and education, not income or consumption.
  • Ecological inference: results are about places, not individual households.
  • The RWI was estimated around 2021 from 2010s surveys and imagery; the census is from 2020.
  • A 500 m buffer is a modelling choice for embedding features.
  • Language- and household-based census measures undercount people who self-identify as Indigenous.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
• Cities: use the AGEB (census tract) tables and the INEGI geostatistical framework to place urban population inside tiles.
  • Change over time: compare 2020 maps with the next census or intercensal survey.
  • Other countries: Guatemala, Peru and Bolivia publish censuses with Indigenous identifiers.
  • Other deployed maps: NASA's Global Gridded Relative Deprivation Index (GRDI) can be audited with the same code.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Chouldechova, A. (2017). Fair prediction with disparate impact: a study of bias in recidivism prediction instruments. Big Data, 5(2).
  • Gneiting, T. (2011). Making and evaluating point forecasts. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 106(494).
  • Gneiting, T., & Raftery, A. E. (2007). Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 102(477).
  • Hyndman, R. J., & Koehler, A. B. (2006). Another look at measures of forecast accuracy. International Journal of Forecasting, 22(4).
  • Kleinberg, J., Mullainathan, S., & Raghavan, M. (2017). Inherent trade-offs in the fair determination of risk scores. Innovations in Theoretical Computer Science (ITCS).

Studies of satellite poverty maps that motivate the audit are cited in the pre-analysis plan.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Four models predict the infrastructure-deprivation rate of a rural locality (the share of dwellings lacking electricity, piped water, drainage, or with a dirt floor) from satellite data, trained on a simulated household survey. They exist to study how mapping methods distribute their errors, not to be used for targeting.

Model Inputs Method Night lights (GBM) VIIRS 2020 radiance Histogram gradient boosting Embeddings (GBM) AlphaEarth 2020 embedding (64-d) Histogram gradient boosting Embeddings (GBM + EB) same Boosting plus empirical-Bayes municipality effects from cross-fitted residuals Embeddings (Fay-Herriot) 20 principal components of the embedding Small area estimation with municipality and locality random effects (REML)

docs.title: Intended use
docs.text:
• Research on the accuracy and fairness of poverty maps.
  • Teaching example of small area estimation versus machine learning under a realistic survey design.

docs.title: Out of scope
docs.text:
• Selecting beneficiaries or ranking specific communities for programs.
  • Urban areas (see the scope note in Methods).
  • Years other than 2020 without revalidation.

docs.title: Training data
docs.text: A survey simulated from the 2020 census: 400 municipalities drawn with probability proportional to rural population, 8 localities per municipality, 20 dwellings per locality, localities with at least 10 dwellings only. 20 replications.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Scored on localities the survey did not visit, in each of 20 replications, for Indigenous and non-Indigenous localities separately, per person (population-weighted, primary) and per community (unweighted). Metrics were fixed in advance; the reasons are in Methods → Evaluation metrics.

Aspect Metric Accuracy RMSE (primary: the budget formula needs the mean right), MAE Fairness Signed bias by group (H4: paired difference in absolute bias, boosting minus Fay-Herriot) Compression Calibration slope, variance ratio, bias by true deprivation decile Uncertainty Coverage, width and interval score of 90% conformal intervals (marginal and group-conditional), inside and outside the survey frame Decisions Exclusion error under "poorest 20%" targeting; net shift, misallocation share and municipal percentage error in a FAIS-style budget

MAPE and MSLE are not used: deprivation rates are often zero, and both discount errors in the most deprived places. See Results.

docs.title: Ethical considerations
docs.text: Errors are not evenly distributed: the project exists to measure that. Any reuse of these models should report group-level performance and should involve the communities affected. See Ethics & data sovereignty.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Ground truth describes dwellings, not income.
  • Embeddings are averaged within a fixed 500 m buffer.
  • Performance outside the survey frame (localities with fewer than 10 dwellings) is extrapolation.

docs.title: Pre-analysis plan
docs.text:
Status

Version 1. Upload this file and create the tag pap-v1 before running any real-data step past the build (GitHub → Releases → Draft a new release → Choose a tag → type pap-v1 → Create new tag on publish). The tag's timestamp is the record that hypotheses and specifications came first. Later changes go in the deviations log with a reason, never by editing the text above it.

docs.title: 1. Motivation
docs.text:
Poverty maps built from satellite imagery and machine learning are used to target cash transfers and infrastructure where surveys are thin. Two strands of evidence motivate this audit:

  • Aiken, Rolf & Blumenstock (IJCAI 2023) find urban-rural bias in satellite poverty maps, using Mexican data among others, and show the bias distorts allocations.
  • Corral, Henderson & Segovia (Journal of Development Economics, 2025) find that machine-learning poverty maps of Mexico are less accurate than small area estimation and most biased for the poorest areas.

Neither examines Indigenous status. Indigenous communities in Mexico are disproportionately poor, rural and remote, so a map can misrank them for reasons that have nothing to do with Indigeneity. The design below separates those reasons.

docs.title: 2. Hypotheses
docs.text:
All hypotheses are about rural localities (fewer than 2,500 inhabitants; see §3). "Indigenous share" is the share of the population living in Indigenous census households (PHOG_IND / POBTOT). An "Indigenous locality" or "Indigenous tile" has a share of at least 40%.

ID Hypothesis Primary metric Test H1 Representation Indigenous localities are less likely to fall inside an RWI tile, holding size and remoteness fixed. Coefficient on Indigenous share in a linear probability model of coverage Two-sided, municipality-clustered SEs; Holm-adjusted p < 0.05 H2 Rank bias Within the same true wealth decile, the RWI ranks Indigenous tiles as wealthier than the census does. Coefficient on Indigenous share in specification 5 of §5 (percentile points) One-sided (coefficient > 0), municipality-clustered SEs; Holm-adjusted p < 0.05 H3 Label choice The share of the Indigenous population counted among the nation's poorest 20% differs across the three labels by at least 5 percentage points. Max − min across labels Descriptive; the census is a full count, so there is no sampling test H4 Challengers In simulated surveys, satellite-embedding gradient boosting has larger absolute bias for Indigenous localities than small area estimation with municipality effects. Paired difference |bias(GBM)| − |bias(Fay-Herriot)|, population-weighted, Indigenous localities, computed within each replication Supported if the 95% range of the paired differences across replications lies above 0 H5 Uncertainty Marginal 90% conformal intervals cover Indigenous localities less than 87% of the time; group-conditional intervals cover them within ±3 points of 90% inside the survey frame. Empirical coverage, unsampled localities Mean over replications with 95% replication range; interval score reported alongside H6 Money Replacing census data with the RWI in the FAIS-style formula lowers the allocation to Indigenous-majority municipalities. Net change in pesos and percent Descriptive (full census); misallocation share reported alongside

Multiple testing. H1 and H2 are the confirmatory hypotheses; their p-values are adjusted together with Holm's method and each is supported if its adjusted p-value is below 0.05. H3 to H6 are reported as estimates with uncertainty ranges, not as tests.

Directional caveat. H2 is stated in the direction suggested by prior work, but a negative coefficient (the map overstates Indigenous deprivation) would be reported with equal prominence.

docs.title: 3. Data and sample
docs.text:
• Ground truth: INEGI 2020 census, results by locality (ITER). Localities with fewer than three dwellings have suppressed characteristics and are excluded from label construction.
  • Scope: rural localities (fewer than 2,500 people). ITER provides one coordinate per locality, so a city would fall into a single 2.4 km tile; RWI tiles that contain any urban locality are dropped from the tile-level audit.
  • Map under audit: Meta's Relative Wealth Index for Mexico, joined by quadkey.
  • Satellite features: AlphaEarth Foundations embeddings for 2020 (mean within 500 m of each locality) and VIIRS 2020 night lights.

docs.title: 4. Variables
docs.text: Variable Definition wealth_dhs_like First principal component of 8 durable goods and 4 housing services (primary label for the RWI audit) dep_infra Mean share of dwellings without electricity, piped water, drainage, or with a dirt floor (target for challengers and allocation) marg_index First principal component of 8 CONAPO-style marginalization indicators rank_error 100 × (RWI percentile − census wealth percentile) among tiles, population-weighted. Positive = map ranks the tile wealthier than the census Controls log tile population, urban share (dropped if constant), log km to the nearest city of 50,000+, altitude, true wealth decile, state

docs.title: 5. Primary specification (H2)
docs.text:
Weighted least squares on tiles, weights = tile population, standard errors clustered by municipality:

\[ \text{rank\_error}_t = \beta \,\text{IndShare}_t + \gamma' X_t + \delta_{\text{decile}(t)} + \alpha_{\text{state}(t)} + \varepsilon_t \]

Specifications 1-4 add controls cumulatively and are reported to show how much of the raw gap is explained by rurality, remoteness and true wealth. Specification 5 is the confirmatory one.

docs.title: 6. Evaluation metrics
docs.text:
Each metric matches the decision the map feeds. Full rationale: Methods → Evaluation metrics.

Question Primary metric Also reported Does the map misrank Indigenous places? (H2) Indigenous minus non-Indigenous rank error among equally poor tiles (the §5 coefficient) The same gap among tiles the map ranks the same (by map decile) How accurate is a challenger? (H4) RMSE of the predicted deprivation rate MAE Is a challenger fair? (H4) Signed bias for Indigenous localities Bias by true deprivation decile, calibration slope, variance ratio Are the intervals honest? (H5) Coverage by group Interval (Winkler) score, width Where does the money go? (H6) Net change for Indigenous-majority municipalities Misallocation share (half the sum of absolute differences in budget shares); median absolute percentage error by municipality
  • RMSE first. The budget formula sums predicted rates, so predictions must get the mean right, and squared error is the loss whose best prediction is the mean. MAE is secondary.
  • No MAPE or MSLE on rates. Many localities have a deprivation rate of zero, where MAPE is undefined, and both measures discount errors in the most deprived places. Percentage errors are used only for municipal allocations, which are never zero.
  • People and places. Every challenger metric is reported population-weighted (primary) and unweighted.
  • Compression. The calibration slope (truth regressed on prediction) and the ratio of prediction to truth variance are reported for every model and group, because a model can lower its RMSE by pulling predictions toward the average.
  • Two views of rank error. The separation view (by true decile) is confirmatory. The calibration view (by map decile) is secondary, and is compared with its value in a synthetic world without planted bias, because groups that differ in average wealth show a gap in this view even when the map's errors ignore group.
  • Paired comparisons. Models are compared on the same simulated survey within each replication.
  • Denominators. Each analysis reports the share of the in-scope population it covers, by group, with localities whose census data are suppressed as a separate group.

docs.title: 7. Robustness (reported regardless of outcome)
docs.text:
1. Unweighted regressions.
  2. Language-based Indigenous share (P3YM_HLI / P_3YMAS) instead of the household measure.
  3. Thresholds of 30% and 50% for "Indigenous".
  4. Excluding tiles with fewer than 50 people.
  5. The same audit with each of the other ground truths: infrastructure deprivation, the rebuilt marginalization index, and the official CONAPO marginalization index if the file is available.

Each check re-estimates specification 5; mapaudit robustness (notebook 03) writes them to results/real/tables/robustness.csv.

docs.title: 8. Simulation design (H4, H5)
docs.text: 20 replications. Each draws 400 municipalities with probability proportional to rural population, 8 localities per municipality, and 20 dwellings per locality, among localities with at least 10 dwellings. Models: night lights (GBM), embeddings (GBM), embeddings (GBM + empirical-Bayes municipality effects), embeddings (Fay-Herriot with municipality random effect, 20 principal components). Metrics are computed on localities the survey did not visit, for each replication, and summarized by their mean and 2.5th-97.5th percentiles across replications.

docs.title: 9. What would change the conclusions
docs.text:
• If the H2 coefficient shrinks to zero once the true decile is controlled for, the gap is a "poorest places get compressed" problem, not an Indigenous-specific one. That is still a finding, with a different remedy.
  • If the gap appears among places the map ranks the same but not among equally poor places, the map's errors are not group-specific, yet its ranking still cannot be taken at face value for Indigenous places. The remedy is then group-aware calibration or small area estimation, not a better map.
  • If the RWI's quadkey join fails for more than 5% of tiles, the audit stops until the cause is found.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text: Three ways to run the project, from least to most setup.

docs.title: 1. In your browser (synthetic demo, nothing to install)
docs.text: Runs the whole pipeline on synthetic data with planted biases, in about two minutes.

docs.title: 2. JupyterLab (the full analysis)
docs.text:
Requirements: Python 3.11 or newer, about 8 GB of RAM and 5 GB of disk, and for the satellite step a Google Cloud project registered for Earth Engine (free for noncommercial use).

Open the project folder in JupyterLab and run the notebooks in order:

Notebook What it does Time 00_setup Installs dependencies, personalizes the files, runs the checks, puts the project on GitHub 5 min 01_demo Every step on synthetic data 2 min 02_ground_truth Downloads the census and the wealth map; builds and sanity-checks the tables 15 min 03_audit Audit of the Relative Wealth Index (H1, H2, H3, H6) and robustness 5 min 04_satellite_features Earth Engine export of AlphaEarth embeddings and night lights 30-90 min (server side) 05_challengers Survey simulation and challenger models (H4, H5) 10-20 min 06_report_and_release Final run, README findings, checks before sharing 25 min

Notebook 04 also runs well in Google Colab, where Earth Engine sign-in and Google Drive are built in.

docs.title: 3. Terminal
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[dev]"
mapaudit demo                 # synthetic run
mapaudit download             # real data into data/raw
mapaudit build && mapaudit audit && mapaudit robustness
mapaudit export-gee --project YOUR_PROJECT   # then download the CSVs into data/raw
mapaudit build && mapaudit simulate && mapaudit report

docs.title: Validation on synthetic data
docs.text:
Synthetic data

Everything on this page comes from synthetic data with biases planted on purpose. It shows that the pipeline runs end to end and that the audit can detect a bias of known size. It says nothing about Mexico. Real results live on the Results page.

docs.title: Does the audit find a planted bias, and only when it is there?
docs.text:
Two fresh synthetic worlds drawn with the demo settings, one with the planted bias and one without. Without it, the coefficient and the equally-poor gap should be near zero. The ranked-equally gap need not be: when groups differ in average wealth, a map whose errors ignore group still shows a gap among places it ranks the same (see Methods).

docs.title: Headline numbers
docs.text:
• Rank bias. Holding true wealth decile, settlement size, remoteness, altitude, and state fixed, the map ranks an all-Indigenous tile +20.3 percentile points higher than a non-Indigenous tile relative to the census (95% CI +15.1 to +25.5; one-sided p = 1.14e-14, Holm-adjusted p = 2.28e-14).
  • Within the same true decile, Indigenous tiles' average rank error exceeds non-Indigenous tiles' by +8.6 points (weighted by Indigenous population).
  • Among places the map ranks the same, Indigenous tiles' rank error is +13.8 points higher, i.e. they are poorer than the map says. This view can show a gap even for a map with group-blind errors, because groups differ in average wealth.
  • Coverage. 90.9% of the Indigenous rural population lies inside a map tile, vs. 92.8% of the non-Indigenous rural population.
  • Money. Using the map instead of the census in a FAIS-style formula changes the allocation to Indigenous-majority municipalities by -26.3% (-102.1 million pesos per billion allocated); 11.6% of the whole budget goes to the wrong municipalities.
  • Targeting. Selecting the poorest 20% by the map leaves out 49% of the truly poorest Indigenous population vs. 35% of the truly poorest non-Indigenous population.
